title: UniRestorer: Universal Image Restoration via Adaptively Estimating Image Degradation at Proper Granularity
claim: Existing frameworks either share one backbone, add prompts or adapters, or select experts from fragile estimates; ours adaptively picks an expert at a suitable granularity from a degradation hierarchy.
layout: 4 panels: three prior-method panels (a–c) side by side on top, one large proposed-framework panel (d) below, each in its own color-coded box
description: The figure has four color-tinted panels. The top row has three small panels: (a) a degradation-agnostic framework in pink, with an All Task oval feeding colored arrows into one Encoder and Decoder; (b) a PEFT-based framework in yellow, where the Encoder and Decoder connect to Prompts or Adapters boxes; (c) an expert-based framework in green, where Deg. modules pick expert filters or LoRA modules shown as colored icons in a dashed box. Below, a large blue panel (d) shows the proposed method. Low-quality input photos (rain, blur, snow) enter a Deg. Ext. block that feeds Granularity and Degradation estimators. These select nodes in a three-level tree: a coarse All-tasks node, task nodes (Snow, Rain, Haze), and fine L/M/S nodes. A Coarsest-to-Finest arrow runs alongside the tree. The selected expert goes into a Multi-Granularity MoE Model, which outputs clean HQ predictions. The eye goes first to the large tree in (d).
caption: Illustration of representative all-in-one image restoration frameworks. (a) Degradation-agnostic methods [ref] train a shared backbone using data from all tasks and are limited in leveraging degradation-specific restoration. (b) PEFT-based methods [ref] apply learnable prompts or adapters to the backbone to adapt various tasks. (c) Expert-based methods [ref] train specific MoE, LoRA, or filters for specific tasks. However, both (b) and (c) suffer from the inevitable error in degradation estimation. (d) We construct a multi-granularity degradation set and a multi-granularity MoE restoration model. By adaptively estimating image degradation at proper granularity, our UniRestorer can be effective in leveraging degradation-specific restoration while being robust to degradation estimation error.
abstract: Recently, considerable progress has been made in all-in-one image restoration. Generally, existing methods can be degradation-agnostic or degradation-aware. However, the former are limited in leveraging degradation-specific restoration, and the latter suffer from the inevitable error in degradation estimation. Consequently, the performance of existing methods has a large gap compared to specific single-task models. In this work, we make a step forward in this topic, and present our UniRestorer with improved restoration performance. Specifically, we perform hierarchical clustering on degradation space, and train a multi-granularity mixture-of-experts (MoE) restoration model. Then, UniRestorer adopts both degradation and granularity estimation to adaptively select an appropriate expert for image restoration. In contrast to existing degradation-agnostic and -aware methods, UniRestorer can leverage degradation estimation to benefit degradation specific restoration, and use granularity estimation to make the model robust to degradation estimation error. Experimental results show that our UniRestorer outperforms state-of-the-art all-in-one methods by a large margin, and is promising in closing the performance gap to specific single task models.
